title: Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Meyer, Borgman & Johnson v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2024) held that a Minnesota structural engineering firm's research was funded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), denying roughly $190,000 in federal R&D tax credits. For U.S. contractors, fixed-price contracts requiring only standard-of-care performance are not enough; payment must be expressly or by clear implication contingent on research success.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024) (Docket No. 23-1523, decided May 6, 2024), the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed the decision of the United States Tax Court denying approximately $190,000 in federal research and development (R&D) tax credits claimed by a structural engineering firm. The decision represents a watershed moment in United States federal tax jurisprudence governing the "funded research" exclusion under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C. or 26 U.S.C.) § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation (26 C.F.R.) § 1.41-4A(d). By requiring that a contract expressly or by clear implication make payment contingent on the success of the research, the Eighth Circuit followed the reasoning of the Fifth Circuit (Grigsby), the Eleventh Circuit (Geosyntec), and the Court of Federal Claims (Dynetics), while distinguishing the Federal Circuit's decision in Fairchild, and held that MBJ's standard professional-services contracts—notwithstanding their fixed prices, phased client approvals, and inspection, acceptance, and quality assurance provisions—did not make payment contingent on the success of MBJ's research, although the court did not hold that fixed-price contracts are per se funded.
Factual and Procedural History

The taxpayer, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ), is a Minnesota-based structural engineering firm engaged in creating structural designs and construction documents for commercial, institutional, and historic building projects. For its fiscal tax years ending September 30, 2010, September 30, 2011, and September 30, 2013 (encompassing the periods from October 1, 2009 through September 30, 2011, and from October 1, 2012 through September 30, 2013), MBJ claimed roughly $190,000 in federal research tax credits under I.R.C. § 41 for wages and expenses incurred by its engineers in developing structural design solutions.

Following an examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued a Notice of Deficiency disallowing the claimed credits in their entirety. MBJ timely petitioned the United States Tax Court (Docket No. 7805-16) to challenge the disallowance. During Tax Court discovery, MBJ and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agreed to evaluate a representative sample of project contracts to resolve the threshold legal question of whether MBJ's engineering activities constituted "funded research." The sampled agreements primarily consisted of fixed-price (stipulated sum) professional service contracts under which MBJ designed structural systems in exchange for phased payments.

On November 19, 2020, United States Tax Court Judge Mark V. Holmes issued an order granting summary judgment in favor of the Commissioner (an unpublished order in Docket No. 7805-16, after which the Tax Court entered its decision sustaining the disallowance), holding that MBJ's research activities were "funded" by its clients within the meaning of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) because none of the contracts expressly or by clear implication made payment contingent on the technical success of MBJ's research. MBJ appealed the summary judgment ruling to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 7482(a)(1). Reviewing the Tax Court's grant of summary judgment and legal conclusions de novo under Torgerson v. City of Rochester, 643 F.3d 1031, 1042 (8th Cir. 2011), a unanimous Eighth Circuit panel—in an opinion authored by Circuit Judge Duane Benton—affirmed the Tax Court's judgment on May 6, 2024.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal dispute in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson sits at the intersection of the affirmative qualification rules of I.R.C. § 41 and the statutory exclusions designed to prevent duplicate or windfall tax benefits. Under fundamental principles of United States tax law articulated by the Supreme Court in INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992), tax credits and deductions are matters of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of clearly establishing entitlement to the claimed benefit.

Under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer may claim a credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of the taxpayer's "qualified research expenses" (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. To constitute "qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), an activity must satisfy a conjunctive four-part statutory test. First, under the Section 174 Test (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures with respect to the activity must be eligible to be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174, requiring that the activity be intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying fundamentally on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined in I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer), specifically targeting improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)), substantially all (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more) of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation capable of evaluating one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

Even where a contractor's technical engineering activities satisfy all four prongs of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), Congress enacted eight categorical exclusions in I.R.C. § 41(d)(4). Foremost among these for service providers is I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes from the definition of qualified research "[a]ny research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)." Because the statute does not define the term "funded," Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9) directs taxpayers to the cross-referenced provisions of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and the foundational appellate framework established in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), determining whether research performed under a third-party contract is "funded" requires a two-pronged inquiry into the agreements executed between the parties. The first requirement is the Economic Risk or Contingency Prong under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), which dictates that all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons are considered in determining the extent to which the research is funded. However, "[a]mounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding." This creates a statutory "mirror rule" between the researcher and the client: if payment is required regardless of the research outcome, the client may claim 65 percent of the payment as a "contract research expense" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), whereas the researcher is barred from claiming the credit. Conversely, if payment is contingent on the success of the research, the client is purchasing a finished product or result (barring the client from claiming contract research expenses), and the performing contractor retains the right to claim the credit.

The second requirement under the regulatory framework is the Substantial Rights Prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Even if a contractor bears economic risk, if the taxpayer performing research for another person "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded for purposes of section 41(d)(4)(H), and no expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer in performing the research are qualified research expenses." Crucially, the regulation stipulates that "[i]ncidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research," nor does a taxpayer retain substantial rights if it must pay the client a royalty or fee to use the research results in future projects.
The Court's Final Holding and Broader Implications

Neither the Tax Court's summary judgment ruling nor the Eighth Circuit's opinion decided whether MBJ's structural engineering work satisfied the technical four-part definition of "qualified research"; both courts resolved the case solely on whether the activities were disqualified as funded research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). The Eighth Circuit held that MBJ's research was fully funded because its client contracts compensated MBJ for performing professional design services in accordance with a general standard of care rather than conditioning payment on the successful resolution of technological uncertainty.

The second- and third-order ramifications of the MBJ ruling across the United States tax landscape are profound. First, the decision eliminates the long-standing industry assumption that fixed-price or stipulated-sum contracts automatically transfer sufficient financial risk to the contractor to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Second, by elevating the "four corners of the contract" above post-hoc testimony regarding commercial course of dealing, the court empowered IRS exam teams to summarily disallow R&D credit claims during the initial stages of an audit based solely on standard commercial contract templates (such as unmodified American Institute of Architects (AIA) or Engineers Joint Contract Documents Committee (EJCDC) forms) without ever evaluating the underlying engineering merits. Subsequent United States Tax Court decisions have continued this trend: in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), the court repeatedly cited MBJ, rejected a post-Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo validity challenge to the funded research regulations of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), and found that none of the sample project contracts made payment contingent on the success of the research (while holding that the taxpayers retained substantial rights in four of the six sample projects, allowing partial credits for those projects), whereas Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, denied an engineering firm's credits on substantiation and qualified-research grounds rather than under the funded research exclusion.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of MBJ's research tax credits stemmed from specific contractual and evidentiary deficiencies within the sampled project agreements. Rather than presenting contracts structured around uncertain technological development and line-item technical acceptance, MBJ presented standard professional service agreements that insulated the firm from true research failure risk.
Conflation of "Proper Performance" with "Successful Performance"

The primary legal failure in MBJ's position was its attempt to equate a professional engineer's obligation to adhere to a general "standard of care" and local building codes with a contractual mandate to achieve "successful research." In its briefs, MBJ argued that its right to payment was contingent on research success because its contracts required the firm to design structural systems that met all owner program requirements, complied with applicable building codes and zoning regulations, and adhered to the professional standard of care—specifically promising work free from negligence, error, or defects.

The Eighth Circuit dismantled this argument by adopting the analytical framework of the Eleventh Circuit in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330, 1340–41 (11th Cir. 2015). Judge Benton, quoting Geosyntec, explained that there is a difference between "proper performance"—which involves providing professional deliverables pursuant to a general professional standard of care, complying with pertinent building codes and regulations, and promising services free from professional negligence, error, or defects—and "successful performance," which requires meeting detailed barometers of success.

Citing Geosyntec, 776 F.3d at 1341, the Eighth Circuit ruled that contractual requirements to comply with pertinent codes and regulations or to perform pursuant to a general standard of care does "not mandate success." In professional engineering, the standard of care requires only that an engineer exercise the degree of skill and diligence ordinarily employed by members of the profession under similar circumstances. If an engineer conducts an experimental design effort with due care and free from negligence, but the novel structural concept ultimately proves technically infeasible, the engineer has still rendered "proper performance" and remains legally entitled to compensation unless the contract explicitly shifts the risk of technological infeasibility to the engineer. Furthermore, the Eighth Circuit observed that many of MBJ's contracts stated that MBJ was "responsible for methods and means used in performing its services" consistent with the general standard of care. Far from proving contingency, leaving the design methods and means almost entirely to the consultant's professional expertise subject only to general, passive owner requirements demonstrates that the client is purchasing professional labor and expertise rather than a guaranteed technological breakthrough.
Deficient Inspection, Acceptance, and Termination Provisions Under the Fairchild Standard

To bolster its claim that payment was contingent on success, MBJ pointed to contractual provisions allowing clients to inspect design documents at various project phases, requiring quality assurance reviews, and permitting either party to terminate the agreement upon not less than seven days' written notice should the other party "fail substantially to perform." MBJ contended that these mechanisms placed it in the same legal position as the defense contractor in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1996), the landmark case in which the Federal Circuit held that a contractor's fixed-price incentive contract with the United States Air Force to develop the T-46A Next Generation Trainer aircraft was unfunded.

Both Judge Holmes in the Tax Court and Judge Benton in the Eighth Circuit rejected the comparison, holding that MBJ's contracts lacked the requisite specificity of Fairchild. In Fairchild, the contract contained over 1,000 pages of detailed technical specifications that required the contractor to meet specific design, construction, quality, and performance standards. Crucially, the Fairchild court emphasized that the contractor remained at risk for each line item until the research was successfully completed and the product of the research was accepted, and the contract's financing provisions provided that, if Fairchild was making satisfactory progress, the Air Force would pay bimonthly refundable advances termed "progress payments."

In stark contrast, MBJ's contracts closely resembled the disqualified agreements in Dynetics, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492, 505, 515–16 (2015). While MBJ's contracts granted clients a procedural right to review or inspect drawings at phase milestones (such as Schematic Design, Design Development, and Construction Documents), the Eighth Circuit, agreeing with the Tax Court, found that MBJ's contracts lacked the specificity of Fairchild and the express terms that courts have identified as important to establish that payment was contingent on the success of the research. First, the inspection clauses lacked explicit rejection language tied to technical benchmarks, failing to define objective, quantifiable barometers of success upon which the client could legally reject the engineering research and refuse payment. Second, the agreements failed to condition payment strictly on technical acceptance; as in Dynetics, which the Eighth Circuit cited, the contracts did not limit payment to work the client accepted. Moreover, termination for "substantial failure to perform" is a standard commercial breach-of-contract remedy for abandonment or gross negligence, and in standard A&E agreements, if a project is terminated prior to completion, the engineer remains entitled to payment for all "services rendered" up to the date of termination. Third, the contracts lacked any refund or clawback provisions. The Eighth Circuit explicitly noted that "MBJ does not cite any provisions requiring it to refund payments already received if it failed to meet specific benchmarks." Without a legally enforceable clawback obligation requiring the disgorgement of prior progress payments upon ultimate technical failure, periodic milestone payments operate as unconditional client funding.
Collapse of the Fixed-Price Safe Harbor and Conflation of Commercial Risk with Research Risk

As a fallback position, MBJ argued that its research was unfunded because its contracts utilized a fixed-price fee structure. To support this proposition, MBJ relied heavily on an unpublished Tax Court summary judgment order in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 405-17, 2019 WL 13032526, at *2 (T.C. Dec. 6, 2019), which had stated that "[i]n general, fixed priced contracts have been considered unfunded research, qualifying the contractor for the credit." MBJ asserted that because a fixed-price contract caps the total fee, any unexpected engineering iterations or design failures force the firm to absorb the extra labor hours, thereby placing the financial risk of the research on MBJ.

The Eighth Circuit dismantled this theory by relying on the Fifth Circuit's persuasive rationale in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602, 618–20 (5th Cir. 2023). In Grigsby, the taxpayer argued that its fixed-price engineering, procurement, and construction contracts were unfunded because payment was contingent on delivering a "result or product" and because fixed-price contracts are "inherently risky." The Fifth Circuit rejected both arguments, and the Eighth Circuit relied on that reasoning in MBJ, noting the Fifth Circuit's fuller statement that fixed-price contracts are only "more likely to be deemed unfunded" because the researcher may bear the financial risk of failure. First, taxpayers may not conflate "contracts for products or services" with "amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Every commercial service contract requires the delivery of some work product (such as stamped blueprints or specifications) in exchange for a fee, and conditioning payment on the delivery of construction documents is merely a condition of commercial performance rather than a condition that the underlying research succeed in overcoming a technological uncertainty.

Second, the court emphasized the critical distinction between commercial cost-of-performance risk and research failure risk. The Eighth Circuit recognized that MBJ's contracts carried "the general economic risk of investing resources without a commitment to be paid" (citing Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 515–16). However, the risk of underbidding a fixed-price contract, experiencing labor inefficiencies, or suffering cost overruns that erode profit margins is ordinary commercial "cost-of-performance risk." Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) as applied in MBJ, the question is whether the contract expressly or by clear implication makes payment contingent on the success of the research—for example, through detailed technical specifications, explicit rejection language, a limitation of payment to accepted work, or an obligation to refund payments already received if specific benchmarks are not met. Because MBJ's fixed-price contracts lacked express rejection and non-payment clauses tied to technical failure, the fixed-price label could not salvage the claim.
Intersecting Vulnerabilities: Substantial Rights, Funding Allocation, and Substantiation

While the Eighth Circuit disposed of MBJ's claim entirely under the economic risk prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), the court's analysis—including its closing citation to Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—highlights the broader matrix of legal hurdles facing contract researchers. Under the conjunctive regulatory scheme of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), even if a contractor incurs total research expenses that exceed the client's unconditional funding (which under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) could theoretically permit a pro-rata allocation where funding stacks first against at least 65 percent of otherwise creditable QREs), the contractor is barred from claiming any partial credit if it fails the "substantial rights" test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). As illustrated in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1 (where the Tax Court held the research on one project funded because the taxpayer did not retain substantial rights), and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (where the Tax Court found substantial rights retained in four of six sample projects based on the taxpayer's retention of copyrights or license agreements, but not in the remaining two), the intellectual property provisions of client agreements—such as "work-made-for-hire" or blanket intellectual property assignment clauses that transfer exclusive ownership of all drawings, calculations, and underlying design methodologies to the client—can be decisive. If the engineering firm retains only "incidental benefits" (such as general professional know-how or experience) rather than an enforceable, royalty-free right to use the specific research results in its own business, the project is 100 percent disqualified with zero proration.

Furthermore, although the Eighth Circuit cited Little Sandy Coal only with a "see generally" signal and did not decide whether MBJ's activities constituted qualified research, the citation is a reminder that surviving contract review is merely the price of admission. Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the taxpayer must still substantiate through contemporaneous documentation—rather than generalized employee interviews or phase-based accounting codes—that at least 80 percent ("substantially all") of the activities applied to each discrete business component (or shrunk-back subcomponent under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) constituted a structured, scientific-method-like process of experimentation.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement governing the Meyer, Borgman & Johnson dispute against the taxpayer's specific legal arguments and contractual deficiencies, alongside the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Eighth Circuit and related federal appellate precedent.

Court's Standard of Proof & Controlling Precedent

cells: Burden of Proof for Tax Credits
I.R.C. § 41(a)(1); Tax Court Rule 142(a)

MBJ contended that its contracts required it to create designs meeting all owner requirements and pertinent codes and regulations, and that termination provisions for failure to substantially perform made its right to payment contingent on the success of its research.

Tax credits are a matter of legislative grace; the taxpayer bears the burden of clearly showing the right to the claimed benefit (INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992), quoted in Zavadil v. Commissioner, 793 F.3d 866, 869 (8th Cir. 2015); Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, 100 F.4th at 988).
Funded Research Exclusion (Payment Contingent on Success)

MBJ argued that its right to payment was contingent on research success because clients only paid if MBJ delivered designs meeting owner requirements and building codes. As the Tax Court found, none of the contracts expressly or by clear implication made payment contingent on the success of MBJ's research.

To be treated as an unfunded payment for a "product or result," the agreement must expressly or by clear implication condition the right to payment on the technical success of the research itself, not merely the delivery of professional services (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); MBJ, 100 F.4th at 989).
Successful Performance vs. Proper Performance (Standard of Care)
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)

MBJ relied on contract clauses requiring compliance with local building codes, zoning laws, and a general professional "standard of care" (promising work free from negligence, error, or defects) where MBJ controlled the "methods and means" of design.

Compliance with building codes and a professional standard of care constitutes "proper performance," which does "not mandate success." Unfunded research requires "successful performance" measured against detailed, objective technical barometers of success (Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330, 1340–41 (11th Cir. 2015); MBJ, 100 F.4th at 989).
Inspection, Acceptance, and Quality Assurance Clauses
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)

MBJ argued that phase-level design reviews, quality assurance procedures, and client rights to terminate for "substantial failure to perform" mirrored the unfunded contract in Fairchild Industries. However, the contracts lacked explicit rejection clauses and refund requirements.

General inspection, acceptance, and termination clauses are insufficient where they lack the specificity of Fairchild and the express terms courts have identified as important, such as highly specific technical specifications, explicit rejection language, limitation of payment to accepted work, and refund obligations for payments already received if specific benchmarks are not met (Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868, 870–74 (Fed. Cir. 1996); Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492, 505 (2015)).
Fixed-Price Contract Structure & Economic Risk Allocation
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)

Citing the unpublished order in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner (2019), MBJ argued that fixed-price contracts are generally considered unfunded because the firm absorbs cost overruns from extra design iterations.

Fixed-price contracts are not per se unfunded. The court distinguishes ordinary commercial "cost-of-performance risk" (investing resources or losing profit margin on a fixed fee) from "research failure risk." Conflating a fixed-price contract for services with payment contingent on research success is legally invalid (United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602, 618–20 (5th Cir. 2023); MBJ, 100 F.4th at 989–90).
Retention of Substantial Rights in Research
Standard A&E contracts often assign ownership of "Instruments of Service" or work product to the owner upon payment, leaving the engineer only with general professional experience.

The taxpayer must retain a legally enforceable, at least non-exclusive right within the contract (including any master agreement) to use the underlying research results in its own business without paying a royalty to the client. Incidental benefits like increased experience do not qualify (Lockheed Martin, 210 F.3d at 1375; Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1; Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50).
Process of Experimentation & Subcomponent Substantiation
Although not reached in MBJ, A&E firms routinely rely on standard multi-phase design workflows (SD, DD, CD) and lump-sum project time logs as evidence of experimentation.

The taxpayer must prove with contemporaneous records that ("substantially all") of activities on a specifically defined business component (or shrunk-back subcomponent) involved a scientific-method evaluation of alternatives to eliminate technological uncertainty (Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), cited in MBJ, 100 F.4th at 990; Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how United States taxpayers and technical tax advisors can operationalize the holdings of Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, the following two industry case studies examine realistic commercial projects that initially suffer from the exact legal and evidentiary defects identified by the Eighth Circuit. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step restructuring of contract terms, project governance, experimentation tracking, and technical documentation to achieve full compliance with I.R.C. § 41 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).
Case Study 1: Structural & Geotechnical Engineering Firm (Seismic Base-Isolation & Deep Foundation System)
Initial Deficient Posture (The MBJ Pitfall)

Apex Structural Engineering, Inc. ("Apex"), a domestic structural engineering corporation, enters into a standard AIA B101/C401-style stipulated-sum contract for $1,200,000 to provide structural engineering services for a 16-story acute-care hospital located in a high-seismic zone with liquefiable alluvial soils. Approximately $850,000 of the fee relates to routine superstructure framing design, while $350,000 involves developing a novel, hybrid triple-friction-pendulum seismic base-isolation and post-tensioned mat foundation system capable of limiting inter-story drift to under Maximum Considered Earthquake () ground motions without exceeding a 48-inch structural mat depth.

Under Apex's original contract, the firm agrees to deliver Schematic Design (SD), Design Development (DD), and Construction Documents (CD) "consistent with the professional skill and care ordinarily provided by structural engineers practicing in the same locality under similar circumstances" and in compliance with the International Building Code (IBC) and ASCE 7. The $1,200,000 fixed fee is billed monthly based on the percentage of phase completion (20% SD, 30% DD, 40% CD, 10% Construction Administration), payable within 30 days of invoice. Either party may terminate the agreement for "substantial failure to perform," in which case Apex remains entitled to payment for all services properly rendered through the date of termination. Furthermore, the contract provides that all drawings, Building Information Modeling (BIM) files, and calculations become the exclusive property of the Hospital Owner upon payment, and Apex's engineers log all hours to a single project phase code ("Project 2026-104: Mercy Hospital - DD Phase").

If audited by the IRS under this initial posture, 100 percent of Apex's claimed QREs will be disallowed under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson. First, the contract conflates "proper performance" (adhering to the standard of care and ASCE 7) with "successful performance." Second, the fixed fee is billed progressively by phase without conditioning payment on achieving the drift benchmark, and there is no refund obligation if the hybrid base-isolation design fails peer review or nonlinear time-history validation. Third, the blanket intellectual property assignment strips Apex of "substantial rights" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Finally, blending $850,000 of routine framing design with $350,000 of experimental foundation design under broad phase codes guarantees failure under the 80 percent "substantially all" rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Little Sandy Coal.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring & Bifurcation of Routine vs. Contingent R&D Scopes

Before executing the agreement, Apex must sever the contract into two legally distinct schedules (or execute a separate Experimental Engineering & Prototype Design Agreement) to isolate the uncertain research component from routine engineering services. Schedule A (Routine Professional Services - $850,000) will cover standard gravity and lateral framing design governed by standard professional care and monthly progress billing, which Apex will exclude entirely from its R&D tax credit computation. Schedule B (Contingent Technical Research & Development Deliverable - $350,000) will explicitly govern the design and validation of the Hybrid Seismic Base-Isolation & Post-Tensioned Mat Subcomponent ("Research Deliverable"). To satisfy the judicial standards of MBJ, Fairchild, and Geosyntec, Schedule B must replace standard A&E boilerplate with the express contractual provisions detailed in the table below.

headers: Remedial Contract Provision (Compliant with MBJ & Fairchild)

cells: Technical Barometers of Success
"Engineer shall design the foundation in accordance with the applicable standard of care, owner program requirements, and local building codes."

"Payment under Schedule B is strictly contingent upon the successful technical achievement of the following quantitative Research Benchmarks ('Technical Acceptance Criteria'): (1) Peak inter-story drift ratio across all 11 suite-scaled ground motion pairs under 3D nonlinear response history analysis; (2) Zero uplift tension exceeding at the soil-mat interface without deep tension micropiles; and (3) Maximum structural mat thickness with punching shear demand-to-capacity ratios ."
Inspection, Rejection & Non-Payment Gate
"Owner may review deliverables at each phase and terminate for substantial failure to perform, paying Engineer for services rendered to date."

"Upon completion of the Schedule B Research Deliverable, Owner and the Independent Seismic Peer Review Panel (ISPRP) shall conduct a formal Technical Acceptance Review. If the Research Deliverable fails to satisfy any of the Technical Acceptance Criteria, Owner shall have the absolute right to reject the Research Deliverable. Engineer acknowledges that proper adherence to the professional standard of care does not entitle Engineer to payment if the Technical Acceptance Criteria are not achieved."
Risk of Rework & Mandatory Clawback / Refund
"Invoices are payable monthly based on percentage of completion. No refund provisions apply."

"All costs of iterative modeling, failed design alternatives, and rework required to achieve the Technical Acceptance Criteria shall be borne solely by Engineer. To the extent Owner advances any conditional interim mobilization or milestone payments under Schedule B, such payments shall remain unliquidated advances; if Engineer fails to achieve final written Technical Acceptance from Owner and the ISPRP, Engineer shall refund 100% of all prior Schedule B payments within thirty (30) days of formal rejection."
Retention of Substantial Rights (IP Clause)
"All Instruments of Service, calculations, and designs shall be deemed works made for hire and are assigned exclusively to Owner."

"While Owner receives a license to utilize the physical construction drawings to construct the specific Project, Engineer expressly retains full ownership and a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free, non-exclusive right to use, reproduce, and commercialize all underlying research results, analytical methodologies, parametric finite element scripts, isolator damping algorithms, and engineering techniques developed under Schedule B in Engineer's ongoing business without payment or fee to Owner."

body.text: Step 2: Project Governance & Financial Risk Architecture

To reinforce the revised contractual language with operational reality, Apex must restructure its internal project governance and billing mechanics. First, Apex establishes a segregated accounting job number (2026-104-RD-SEISMIC) exclusively for Schedule B activities, ensuring that all qualifying engineering labor hours, cloud high-performance computing (HPC) simulation expenses (qualifying as direct computer rental or supply expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)), and third-party soil-structure interaction testing are booked solely to this cost center. Second, Apex eliminates unconditional monthly progress billing for Schedule B and institutes two formal Technical Acceptance Gates: Gate 1 covering Soil-Structure Interaction and Isolator Hysteretic Validation, and Gate 2 covering Full 3D Nonlinear Time-History and Mat Shear Validation. Under this governance protocol, no invoice is issued—or any interim draw is recorded on Apex's balance sheet strictly as an unearned, refundable customer deposit liability—until the Independent Seismic Peer Review Panel signs a formal Certificate of Technical Benchmark Acceptance verifying that the exact quantitative metrics in Schedule B have been satisfied.
Step 3: Subcomponent Identification & Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), and the substantiation mandate of Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group, Apex defines the "Business Component" not as the entire hospital building, nor even the entire structural engineering package, but specifically as the Hybrid Seismic Base-Isolation and Post-Tensioned Mat Subcomponent. Prior to commencing design work, the Principal Structural Engineer executes a contemporaneous Baseline Uncertainty Memorandum documenting why standard ASCE 7 equivalent lateral force procedures and conventional deep pile foundations cannot simultaneously resolve the site's liquefiable soil profile, the 48-inch excavation depth constraint, and the hospital drift limit, thereby establishing objective design uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3).

Throughout execution, engineers maintain hypothesis-driven iteration logs for every design alternative modeled in PERFORM-3D and CSI SAFE. Each log entry records the specific technical hypothesis being tested (such as evaluating whether pairing triple-friction-pendulum isolators having an effective period with perimeter viscous fluid dampers reduces corner mat uplift below ), the exact simulation parameters and ground motion inputs, the quantitative output metrics demonstrating why the iteration succeeded or failed, and the engineering modifications required for the subsequent trial. Concurrently, Apex enforces granular time-tracking rules that prohibit logging hours to generic design phases; every timesheet entry must reference the specific Schedule B subcomponent and experimental iteration (for example, 2026-104-RD-SEISMIC | Iteration 3 Nonlinear Time-History Modeling & Drift Evaluation - 6.5 hrs), while routine gravity framing and code-compliance reviews are isolated in Schedule A (2026-104-STD), ensuring that well over 80 percent of Schedule B hours constitute a verifiable process of experimentation.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Automation & Material Handling Systems Integrator
Initial Deficient Posture (The MBJ & Grigsby Pitfall)

Vanguard Conveyor & Robotics Corp. ("Vanguard"), a domestic industrial engineering and manufacturing firm, is contracted by a national cold-chain pharmaceutical distributor to design, engineer, and build a custom, high-speed automated robotic sorting and conveyor system operating inside a cryogenic freezer facility. The total contract price is structured as a capped time-and-materials and fixed-fee hybrid of $2,500,000.

Under Vanguard's original purchase order and Master Services Agreement (MSA), Vanguard bills the client monthly for engineering and fabrication hours incurred up to a maximum ceiling of $2,500,000, with 10 percent retainage held until physical delivery of the conveyor hardware at the client's facility. Vanguard warrants that the conveyor system will be "free from defects in workmanship and materials for 12 months" and that all engineering services will be performed "in a workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards." The purchase order grants the client "the right to inspect and witness factory testing of all equipment called for by the contract prior to shipment." Finally, while the two-page project work order is silent on intellectual property, a 2019 Master Services Agreement incorporated by reference contains a boilerplate clause stating that "all inventions, software code, mechanical designs, and technical data conceived or first reduced to practice during the performance of any Work Order shall vest solely in Customer."

Applying the reasoning of MBJ and the authorities on which it relied, Vanguard's initial contract structure is vulnerable on four distinct legal grounds. First, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) as applied in Geosyntec (776 F.3d at 1340–43) and MBJ, capped time-and-materials contracts where the client pays for every hour up to a ceiling place the financial risk of failed engineering approaches squarely on the client, because payment is not contingent on the success of the research, rendering the research funded. Second, even if evaluated as a fixed-price contract for a "product or result," under United States v. Grigsby (86 F.4th at 618–20) and MBJ (100 F.4th at 989–90), delivering a physical product warranted against defects in workmanship is merely "proper performance" of a commercial sales agreement, not payment contingent on research success. Third, the factory inspection clause closely mirrors the provision found insufficient in Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 505) and cited by the Eighth Circuit in MBJ: it grants a procedural right to inspect and test, but contains no explicit rejection language and does not limit payment to work the client accepts. Fourth, the background 2019 MSA overrides the project work order and strips Vanguard of all substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Master Agreement Override & Contractual Risk Reallocation

Before commencing engineering on the cryogenic sorting system, Vanguard must execute a binding First Amendment to Master Services Agreement and Statement of Work (SOW) that explicitly supersedes the 2019 MSA's payment, warranty, acceptance, and intellectual property provisions. Vanguard restructures the transaction from a capped-hour service agreement into a strict At-Risk Performance-Contingent Deliverable Contract by eliminating all time-and-materials billing and separating the uncertain R&D subsystem—the Cryogenic High-Speed Vision-Guided Singulator and Low-Inertia Drive Subsystem ("Cryogenic Singulator Subsystem"), priced at a firm, contingent fee of $600,000—from the standard structural steel framework and commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) accumulation chutes ($1,900,000). The table below details the exact contractual modifications required to bring Vanguard's agreement into compliance with MBJ, Grigsby, and Fairchild.

body.text: Step 2: Governance of Prototype Fabrication & Financial Exposure

To substantiate that Vanguard genuinely bore the financial risk of failure during project execution, Vanguard's internal project governance and revenue recognition procedures must mirror the contract's risk-shifting mechanics. Vanguard finances the working capital for engineering design, custom cryogenic polymer synthesis, and prototype actuator fabrication internally until the 72-hour Cryogenic FAT is successfully completed. At the conclusion of the environmental chamber trial, Vanguard enforces a two-stage engineering sign-off gate requiring both Vanguard's Chief Engineer and the Customer's Vice President of Engineering to execute a Line-Item Technical Acceptance Protocol recording the exact measured throughput (UPM), positional tolerance (mm), decibel level (dBA), and torque variance against the contractual specifications. Only after this formal acceptance instrument is signed does Vanguard's accounting department liquidate any conditional deposit liability, recognize the $600,000 revenue, and issue a final non-refundable invoice.
Step 3: Shrinking-Back Subcomponent Architecture & Experimental Records

To insulate the R&D tax credit claim from a Little Sandy Coal challenge regarding the 80 percent "substantially all" process of experimentation threshold, Vanguard applies Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) prospectively to segregate its work breakdown structure (WBS) into discrete subcomponents. Vanguard designates WBS 1.0 for non-qualifying COTS equipment and standard fabrication (including structural steel supports, safety guarding, power distribution panels, and standard conveyor bed assembly), excluding 100 percent of WBS 1.0 costs from its Section 41 claim. Conversely, Vanguard isolates its experimental development into WBS 2.1 (Qualifying Subcomponent 1: Cryogenic Polymer Actuator & Drive Assembly, targeting mechanical and materials engineering to resolve thermal contraction binding and seal failure at ) and WBS 2.2 (Qualifying Subcomponent 2: Thermal-Compensated Machine Vision & Kinematics Software, targeting computer science and optical algorithm development to eliminate frost-induced optical refraction errors at ).

For WBS 2.1 and WBS 2.2, Vanguard maintains a rigorous scientific-method documentation trail. Mechanical engineers record contemporaneous Design of Experiments (DoE) logs detailing the exact material science uncertainties (such as differential coefficients of thermal expansion between 316L stainless steel shafts and PTFE-composite bearings at ) and documenting sequential physical prototype tests (Prototypes A, B, and C) via CAD revision histories, finite element thermal-stress plots, and high-speed video failure logs from the environmental chamber. Concurrently, software engineers developing the machine vision algorithms link Git version-control commits directly to WBS 2.2, documenting alternative image-filtering and edge-detection hypotheses tested against frost-obscured test cartons alongside quantitative false-reject rate metrics. Finally, all raw materials, custom-machined test gears, and optical sensors consumed or destroyed during failed cryogenic chamber trials are requisitioned under dedicated WBS 2.1 and WBS 2.2 purchase orders and photographed prior to scrapping, creating an unimpeachable audit trail for qualified supply expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b).
5. Synthesis of Legal Conclusions for United States Practitioners

The Eighth Circuit's decision in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), stands as binding authority within the Eighth Circuit (and persuasive authority elsewhere) that the funded research exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) turns on whether the taxpayer's contracts, expressly or by clear implication, make payment contingent on the success of the research. Standard commercial agreements that obligate a service provider or custom manufacturer to adhere to a professional standard of care, comply with building or industry codes, submit to phase inspections, or deliver a finished design for a fixed price only establish "proper performance" and ordinary commercial cost-of-performance risk. To establish that research is unfunded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), taxpayers must proactively draft agreements prior to project execution that define detailed, objective technical barometers of research success, grant the client an explicit contractual right to reject deliverables and withhold payment if those technical benchmarks are not achieved, obligate the researcher to refund any prior milestone advances upon technical failure, and expressly reserve to the researcher a royalty-free, substantial right to utilize the underlying research results in its ongoing trade or business.
